login_with_jwt.note: M2M client_credentials grant. grant_type MUST be 'client_credentials'. Requires a MachineToMachine application.

create_provider.note: Creates an enterprise SSO connector (SAML or OIDC). providerName: 'SAML' or 'OIDC'. config contains IdP metadata/endpoints.

create_application.note: type MUST be one of: Native, SPA, Traditional, MachineToMachine, Protected, SAML. postLogoutRedirectUris MUST be an array (can be empty []).

update_application.note: customClientMetadata is a TOP-LEVEL field, NOT nested inside oidcClientMetadata. app_id in path must match the captured id from create_application.

login_with_password.note: Logto uses the Experience API for password login. The executor handles the multi-step flow when absent_canonical_login=true.

saml_login.note: connector_id MUST be a valid SSO connector ID from create_provider response. Use the captured connector_id, not a placeholder.

metadata.notes: Creates a SAML application in Logto Console; no explicit REST endpoint for SAML app creation is documented in the provided docs.

oidc_jwt.description: When no resource is specified, Logto issues an opaque access token instead of a JWT for general OIDC use cases.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not flag missing JWT claims or inability to locally validate signature/audience as a bug when the request omitted resource.

oidc_jwt.description: Permission changes do not modify already-issued JWTs; only newly issued tokens reflect updated permissions.
oidc_jwt.note: A stale old token after role change is by design; test coherence using newly issued tokens.

oidc_jwt.description: For global API resources, newly granted permissions may not appear through refresh unless they were part of the original requested scope set; a new authorization flow may be required.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat absence of newly granted scopes on refresh alone as stale-cache vulnerability.

oidc_jwt.description: Organization tokens are not fetched directly from the authorization code flow; they are obtained via refresh token flow or client credentials with organization parameters.
oidc_jwt.note: A missing organization token immediately after code exchange is expected behavior.

oidc_jwt.description: Existing JWTs keep previously granted scopes until they expire, even after permissions are reduced.
oidc_jwt.note: Only newly issued tokens reflect permission reductions.

oidc_jwt.description: A newly issued token can only include scopes that were requested in the original OAuth authorization flow.
oidc_jwt.note: Missing newly granted scopes after refresh can be by design if they were not in the original request.

oidc_jwt.description: Existing users are automatically linked to enterprise SSO identities when the working email matches an existing Logto account.
oidc_jwt.note: Identity merges on matching email are by design and should not be flagged as cross-user collision without evidence of incorrect email matching.

oidc_jwt.description: Once an email domain is associated with an enterprise SSO connector, existing users with that domain are restricted to sign in with the enterprise SSO connector and previous sign-in methods are blocked.
oidc_jwt.note: A previously valid password or verification-code login failing after SSO domain association is expected policy behavior, not flow incoherence.

oidc_jwt.description: JWT access tokens are bearer tokens and the docs do not describe jti replay tracking for JWT validation.
oidc_jwt.note: Reusing the same valid JWT is not by itself evidence of a freshness bug in a stateless verifier.

oidc_jwt.description: End-session clears centralized session, but grants with offline_access may remain valid until grant TTL expiry.
oidc_jwt.note: Successful refresh after browser logout can be by design when offline_access was granted.

oidc_jwt.description: When no resource is specified, Logto may issue an opaque access token instead of a JWT.
oidc_jwt.note: This affects token format and validation path; it is not an audience-binding bug.

oidc_jwt.description: If a default API resource is configured, Logto uses it as the audience when the resource parameter is omitted.
oidc_jwt.note: Acceptance without an explicit resource may be expected due to tenant default configuration.

oidc_jwt.description: MFA validation is bypassed for users signing in via enterprise SSO because the upstream IdP is treated as trusted.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat absence of a second Logto MFA step after enterprise SSO as a bypass vulnerability.

oidc_jwt.description: Existing JWTs keep their old scopes until they expire even after permissions are reduced.
oidc_jwt.note: Only newly issued tokens reflect permission reductions immediately.

oidc_jwt.description: If direct sign-in fails because the connector is not found or not enabled, Logto falls back to the standard sign-in page.
oidc_jwt.note: A redirect to the normal sign-in page is expected fallback behavior, not flow confusion.

oidc_jwt.constraint: The authorization endpoint is /oidc/auth and returns redirects as part of the browser flow. The fuzzer MUST treat start_oidc_auth as a redirect-producing endpoint and MUST NOT auto-follow redirects when testing OIDC flow coherence or request-parameter injection.

Logto's OIDC userinfo endpoint is /oidc/me, not the more common /userinfo path. verify_granted_identity MUST call /oidc/me with the Bearer access token; using an id_token or a guessed /userinfo path will produce false failures.

For I5 audience-binding tests on JWT access tokens, the fuzzer MUST request a specific API resource using the resource parameter. If no resource is specified, Logto may issue an opaque access token instead of a JWT, which changes validation behavior and invalidates JWT-specific test assumptions.

When no resource is specified in the authorization or token request, Logto issues an opaque access token for general OIDC use cases. JWT-focused tests for aud, iss, exp, custom claims, and organization context MUST include resource and/or organization parameters so the returned access token is a JWT.

For I5 empty_audience and audience_mismatch tests, Logto requires the resource parameter to exactly match the registered API identifier (resource indicator URI). Do NOT use prefixes, shortened names, or wildcard-like values; exact URI matching is required.

Scope names must exactly match the permission names defined for the API resource. There is no wildcard or prefix matching. For I5 authorization-binding tests, the fuzzer MUST request exact scope strings and MUST NOT assume read or write prefixes broaden to read:* or write:* semantics.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests, include a control token request/login in the same scenario using a valid token configuration. Otherwise, a failed attack case may be caused by missing resource, missing organization context, disabled grant type, or wrong client configuration rather than time validation.

Organization tokens cannot be fetched directly from the authorization code flow. To test organization-scoped JWT behavior, the fuzzer MUST first obtain a refresh token (or use client_credentials for M2M) and then call /oidc/token with grant_type=refresh_token or grant_type=client_credentials plus organization_id. Treating the direct code exchange as the organization-token issuance step will cause false negatives.

For organization-level API resource tests, the fuzzer MUST include both resource and organization_id in the token request. If organization_id is omitted, Logto evaluates only global roles/permissions and organization RBAC is not enforced.

For organization non-API permission tests, the fuzzer MUST include organization_id in the token request. Organization permissions are distinct from global API permissions and cannot be mixed with global API permissions in a single authorization assumption.

For I5 scope-escalation tests after permission changes, Logto enforces a scope subset rule: a newly issued access token can only include scopes that were requested in the original OAuth authorization flow. The fuzzer MUST distinguish 'permission granted but not originally requested' from 'authorization binding failure'; enlarged scopes may require a new authorization flow, not just refresh.

For I3 config-change sequences involving permission changes, existing JWTs are BY DESIGN unchanged until expiry. A valid coherence test must compare newly issued tokens after the config change, not expect already-issued JWTs to mutate in place.

For global API resources, enlarged permissions do NOT appear through refresh unless they were already within the originally requested scope set; a new OAuth authorization flow may be required. The fuzzer MUST NOT flag this as stale-cache behavior when testing I3 permission propagation.

For organization tokens, enlarged permissions can appear on next issuance via refresh or token request, but still only within the originally requested scope set. The fuzzer MUST request the target scopes up front if it plans to test later permission expansion.

Token exchange is disabled by default per application. Before running RFC 8693 token_exchange tests, the target application MUST have 'Allow token exchange' enabled, otherwise failures are expected and are not security findings.

For PAT-based or impersonation-style token exchange tests, /oidc/token accepts different subject_token_type values with different semantics. The fuzzer MUST set subject_token_type exactly to the documented value for the token being exchanged (for example urn:logto:token-type:personal_access_token for PATs). Using the wrong token type will cause expected rejection.

For token exchange tests using confidential clients, client authentication may be supplied via HTTP Basic auth or request-body client_id/client_secret depending on client type. The fuzzer MUST use a client authentication mode compatible with the application type; otherwise token exchange failures are setup errors, not invariant violations.

For I5 token_exchange_wrong_audience and token_exchange_ignore_audience tests, the fuzzer SHOULD request a subject token whose aud/resource is explicitly set, then attempt exchange at a different target audience or application. Without an explicitly audience-bound subject token, cross-audience acceptance cannot be interpreted reliably.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, compare the exchanged token's scopes and claims against the original authorization intent. Logto documents that exchanged access tokens obtained from PATs behave identically to refresh-token-derived tokens for organization context and permissions; therefore any broader result must be evaluated against original requested scope/resource/organization context, not just current user role assignments.

Logto supports OIDC discovery at /oidc/.well-known/openid-configuration and publishes issuer and jwks_uri there. For I1 trust-anchor and issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer SHOULD derive issuer and JWKS from discovery rather than hardcoding tenant values, except when intentionally testing issuer mismatch.

Issuer validation is expected against https://<tenant>/oidc. For I1 trust_anchor_substitution tests, the forged token's iss must differ from the configured issuer while preserving other plausible claims; otherwise the test may collapse into a generic signature failure rather than issuer-binding validation.

Several Logto validation examples manually disable library-level audience verification and instruct applications to verify audience based on permission model. Therefore, when testing downstream APIs built from these docs, the fuzzer MUST explicitly check whether the sample app under test implemented audience validation; acceptance of wrong-audience tokens may reflect incomplete sample integration rather than Logto server behavior.

For I5 organization-context tests, validate both audience and organization_id. Logto documentation explicitly requires checking organization context in addition to scopes; a token with correct scopes but wrong or missing organization_id should not be treated as valid for organization-scoped resources.

For sign-out and freshness tests, revoking a token via /oidc/token/revocation does not necessarily revoke all grants in the same way as end-session. Logto sign-out behavior is multi-layered: local client state, centralized session, and grants differ. The fuzzer MUST distinguish token revocation from browser session termination when interpreting post-revocation behavior.

If offline_access was granted, end-session does not revoke that app grant by default; refresh-token chains may remain valid until grant expiration. Therefore, I2/I3 tests that expect global logout to invalidate all future token refreshes MUST account for offline_access or they will produce false positives.

Current SDK signOut behavior is effectively global sign-out through /session/end and /session/end/confirm, but native/sessionless clients may only clear local storage. The fuzzer MUST not assume identical logout semantics across client types when testing session coherence.

For I5 audience-binding tests, the `resource` parameter in `/oidc/auth` and `/oidc/token` MUST exactly match the registered API identifier URI. Logto documentation explicitly states there is no wildcard or prefix matching for scopes/resources; mismatched or shortened values are not equivalent.

For I5 empty-audience and JWT-vs-opaque-token tests, if no `resource` is specified, Logto may issue an opaque access token instead of a JWT. The fuzzer MUST request a `resource` when it needs a JWT access token for API audience validation. Without `resource`, failures may reflect token format differences rather than audience enforcement.

For I5 default-audience behavior, if the tenant has a default API resource configured, omitting `resource` causes Logto to use that default audience. The fuzzer MUST control whether a default API exists before interpreting omitted-`resource` results as 'accepts any audience'.

For I2 expired-token and future-token tests against Logto-issued JWTs, use a control token alongside the attack token. A valid control should use normal issuance through `/oidc/token`; otherwise a rejection may be caused by bad client configuration, missing resource, or unsupported flow rather than time-claim enforcement.

For I5 organization-context tests, `organization_id` changes authorization semantics. If `organization_id` is omitted, only global roles/permissions are evaluated; if present, organization roles are evaluated. The fuzzer MUST keep `organization_id` fixed when testing non-organization authorization invariants, or results will reflect intended context switching rather than a bug.

For I5 mixed-scope tests, Logto documentation states organization permissions cannot be mixed with global API permissions in the same authorization model. The fuzzer MUST NOT interpret rejection of mixed global and organization permission requests as a vulnerability.

For I5 permission-change sequences, Logto JWTs are immutable after issuance. Permission updates only appear in newly issued tokens and never modify existing JWTs. The fuzzer MUST obtain a new token after role/permission changes; testing an old token after admin changes is not a valid stale-authorization oracle.

For I3 config-change sequences involving enlarged permissions, Logto enforces a scope subset rule: a later token can only include scopes that were requested in the original OAuth authorization flow. The fuzzer MUST request the superset of scopes in the original authorization if it plans to test later permission enlargement; otherwise missing scopes are by design.

For I3 organization-token tests, Logto does not support fetching organization tokens directly from the authorization code flow. The fuzzer MUST use refresh-token flow or client-credentials flow with `organization_id` to obtain organization tokens; expecting an org token directly from code flow is invalid setup.

For I1/I5 token-exchange tests, token exchange is disabled by default per application. The fuzzer MUST enable token exchange on the target application before using grant_type `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, or failures are expected configuration errors.

For I2 replay tests on JWT bearer access tokens, do NOT flag reuse of the same JWT as a vulnerability by itself. Logto documentation describes JWT access tokens as standard bearer tokens; replay resistance via jti tracking is not documented and stateless reuse is by design for ordinary access tokens.

For I1 OIDC request-object tests (`request` parameter on `/oidc/auth`), the documentation only states support for the standard authorization endpoint and optional request JWT parameter, but does not document request-object signature policy. The fuzzer SHOULD test `alg=none`, but MUST treat acceptance as meaningful only if the application is expected to require signed request objects.

For I1 issuer-validation tests in resource servers, Logto guidance requires validating `iss` against the tenant issuer from `/.well-known/openid-configuration` or `/oidc`. The fuzzer MUST use the exact issuer URL `https://<tenant>/oidc`; using the tenant root URL without `/oidc` is incorrect setup.

For I1 audience-validation tests in resource servers, several language examples disable library-level audience validation (`verify_aud: false` / `ValidateAudience = false`) and instruct developers to verify audience manually based on permission model. The fuzzer MUST distinguish platform token issuance from relying-party API validation logic; a backend that skips audience checks is an application integration flaw, not necessarily a Logto issuance flaw.

For I2 lifetime tests against .NET sample integrations, the sample sets `ClockSkew = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)`. Resource-server acceptance of slightly expired or not-yet-valid tokens may therefore be due to verifier leeway. The fuzzer SHOULD account for up to 5 minutes skew when testing sample-based backends.

Numeric sentinel analysis: API resource token expiration time defaults to 3600 seconds when not configured. The documentation does not define `0` as literal zero or disable, so the fuzzer MUST NOT assume `0` disables expiry or means immediate expiration without explicit API documentation.

Numeric sentinel analysis: one-time token (magic link) `expiresIn` defaults to 10 minutes if unspecified. The documentation does not define `0` or negative values as disable sentinels. The fuzzer MUST use explicit positive values and MUST NOT assume `0` means no expiry.

For I4 identity-linking tests with enterprise SSO, Logto automatically links an enterprise SSO identity to an existing user account when the working email matches. The fuzzer MUST treat same-email account merging as by-design and not as an identity-collision vulnerability.

For I4 enterprise-SSO tests, once an email domain is associated with an enterprise SSO connector, existing users with that domain are restricted to sign in with the enterprise SSO connector and previous sign-in methods are blocked. The fuzzer MUST NOT interpret blocked password/email-code login for those users as session inconsistency or account takeover.

For I4 connector-collision tests, Logto connector `target` values determine identity-provider naming semantics. Different connectors sharing the same `target` can cause account confusion, while the same IdP with different `target` values intentionally creates separate Logto accounts. The fuzzer MUST model connector target values carefully before asserting cross-provider identity merge/collision bugs.

For I4 case-sensitivity tests on usernames, the platform-level environment variable `CASE_SENSITIVE_USERNAME` defaults to `true`. The fuzzer MUST record tenant configuration before interpreting `Admin` vs `admin` behavior; case-sensitive distinction is the default and not a bug.

For I5 custom-claim override tests, Logto built-in token claims cannot be overridden by custom token claim scripts; conflicting custom claims are ignored. The fuzzer MUST NOT treat inability to replace built-in claims like `sub`, `iss`, or `aud` via custom claims as a vulnerability.

For I5 token-exchange scope-escalation tests using PATs, PAT-exchanged access tokens are documented to behave identically to tokens obtained through refresh-token flow. The fuzzer SHOULD compare exchanged-token scopes against the requested scope/resource and original authorization semantics, not against PAT-specific behavior.

For I5 organization token tests, organization tokens are always JWTs and opaque tokens cannot be used as organization tokens. The fuzzer MUST NOT attempt opaque-token organization access and interpret failure as an authorization bug.

Logto's OIDC provider is mounted at /oidc and the UserInfo endpoint is /oidc/me, not /userinfo. The fuzzer MUST use the documented Logto paths exactly: /oidc/auth, /oidc/token, /oidc/token/revocation, /oidc/token/introspection, /oidc/me.

All direct calls to Logto OIDC APIs that send parameters in the request body MUST use application/x-www-form-urlencoded. This applies to /oidc/token, /oidc/token/revocation, and /oidc/token/introspection. Sending JSON will break the test setup.

For I5 audience-binding tests, the resource parameter must EXACTLY match the registered API identifier/resource indicator URI. Logto does not support wildcard, prefix, or shortened scope/resource matching. If the fuzzer wants a token for a specific API, it MUST request the exact registered resource URI.

For I5 scope-binding tests, requested scope names must EXACTLY match the permission names defined for the API resource. Wildcards and prefixes are not supported. For example, requesting 'read' will not match a configured permission 'read:elections'.

For I5 empty_audience and audience_mismatch tests, Logto issues JWT access tokens for API resources only when a resource is specified, or when a default API resource is configured. If no resource is specified and openid is present, Logto may issue an opaque access token for UserInfo instead of a JWT. The fuzzer MUST request a concrete resource when testing JWT audience enforcement.

By design, when no resource is specified, Logto may issue an opaque access token rather than a JWT. Opaque tokens are validated via /oidc/token/introspection and can be used with /oidc/me, but they are not suitable for JWT-claim mutation tests. The fuzzer MUST avoid no-resource requests for oidc_jwt attack cases.

Organization tokens are always JWTs, but Logto does not support fetching organization tokens directly from the authorization code flow. To obtain an organization token for user flows, the fuzzer MUST first obtain a refresh token, then call /oidc/token with grant_type=refresh_token and organization parameters.

For I5 organization authorization tests, organization RBAC is applied only when organization_id is included in the token request. If organization_id is omitted, only global roles/permissions are evaluated. The fuzzer MUST include organization_id when testing organization permissions or organization-level API resources.

For organization-level API resource tests, the fuzzer MUST request both resource and organization_id together. Without organization_id, Logto evaluates only global roles; without resource, the token is not audience-bound to the target API.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against JWT validation in protected APIs, include a CONTROL request using a valid Logto-issued token alongside the ATTACK request. Otherwise, a 401 on the attack path may reflect broken API setup rather than correct exp/nbf enforcement.

For I3 permission-change sequences, Logto JWTs are immutable after issuance. Permission updates only appear in newly issued tokens and never modify existing JWTs. A valid coherence test must compare newly issued tokens before and after the config change, not expect an already-issued JWT to change in place.

For I3 global permission enlargement tests, newly granted scopes that were not part of the original authorization request will NOT appear through refresh alone. The client must perform a new authorization flow to obtain a token containing newly requested scopes. Do not treat missing newly-added scopes after refresh as a security bug.

For I3 global permission tightening tests, newly issued tokens should immediately reflect reduced scopes, but existing JWTs keep old scopes until expiry. The fuzzer MUST use a fresh token after the change when asserting tightened authorization.

For I3 organization permission enlargement tests, enlarged permissions can appear on the next issuance (refresh or token request), but still require a new token. The fuzzer MUST not expect an already-issued organization JWT to gain scopes without reissuance.

For I3 signing-key rotation tests, Logto exposes public keys at /oidc/jwks and supports key rotation. Existing tokens signed by a previous key remain valid until that previous key is removed. The fuzzer MUST distinguish 'new tokens signed with old key still accepted' from 'old already-issued tokens still validate because previous key remains published'.

Never rotate signing keys consecutively when testing coherence. Logto documentation warns that consecutive rotations may invalidate all issued tokens. A valid I3 key-rotation test should perform a single controlled rotation and then test acceptance/rejection behavior.

For OSS deployments, signing-key rotation requires a Logto instance restart before the new key takes effect. If the target is OSS and the fuzzer cannot restart the instance, key-rotation coherence results may be inconclusive.

Token exchange is disabled by default per application. Before any RFC 8693 token_exchange test, the target application MUST have 'Allow token exchange' enabled, otherwise failures are expected and not evidence of correct audience or scope enforcement.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation and token_exchange_wrong_audience tests, Logto token exchange uses the standard /oidc/token endpoint with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. The fuzzer MUST send subject_token and subject_token_type, and if testing audience/resource binding, MUST set resource to the target API identifier.

For PAT-based token exchange tests, subject_token_type must be urn:logto:token-type:personal_access_token. Using the generic access-token subject_token_type will not exercise the documented PAT exchange path.

For impersonation-style token exchange tests using actor context, the act claim is included only if actor_token and actor_token_type are supplied. If the fuzzer wants to verify actor binding, it MUST provide actor_token; otherwise absence of act is by design.

For I4 identity-linking tests involving enterprise SSO, Logto automatically links an enterprise SSO identity to an existing user account when the working email matches. The fuzzer MUST treat same-email account merging as documented behavior, not as an identity collision bug.

For I4 cross-provider identity tests, connector target/identity-provider naming matters. Documentation states that using different connectors with the same target can cause sign-in to the same Logto account, while the same IdP with different targets creates separate accounts. The fuzzer MUST control connector target values carefully before interpreting identity merges or splits.

For I4 case-confusion tests on usernames, Logto has a CASE_SENSITIVE_USERNAME configuration with default true. Results depend on deployment configuration. The fuzzer MUST record whether username matching is case-sensitive before classifying Admin/admin behavior as a collision.

For I2 replay_same_token on JWT bearer access tokens, replay is generally by design for stateless JWT validation. Logto documentation does not describe jti replay tracking for JWT bearer access tokens. The fuzzer MUST NOT report simple reuse of the same JWT as a vulnerability in oidc_jwt mode.

For I1 issuer-validation tests in resource servers, Logto documentation consistently requires issuer validation against the tenant issuer URL and JWKS signature verification. A valid negative test must mutate iss while keeping all other setup correct; otherwise failures may simply reflect malformed token handling.

For OIDC request-object tests (oidc_request_object_alg_none), the provided documentation does not state that Logto supports signed request objects or request parameter validation rules. The fuzzer SHOULD avoid asserting request-object signature vulnerabilities from this corpus alone.

environment_defaults.api_pattern: Logto Management API uses /api/ prefix. User CRUD: /api/users. SSO connectors: /api/sso-connectors. Applications: /api/applications.
environment_defaults.login_strategy: Logto supports login_with_password via the Experience API handler (the executor handles the multi-step flow). For M2M service login, use login_with_jwt with client_credentials grant.
environment_defaults.app_types: Logto application types: Native, SPA, Traditional, MachineToMachine, Protected, SAML. Do NOT use TraditionalWeb or WebApp — use 'Traditional'.
environment_defaults.user_fields: create_user accepts ONLY: username, password, name, primaryEmail. Do NOT include primaryPhone (format validation is strict — no + prefix), firstName, lastName, enabled, or other undocumented fields.
